subject: math
cluster: Draw, construct, and describe geometrical figures and describe the relationships between them
skillName: Drawing Geometric Shapes with Given Conditions
intro: When you are given measurements for a triangle, the conditions may produce exactly one triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle at all. Two rules govern whether a triangle can even exist: the three side lengths must satisfy the triangle inequality (the two shorter sides must add to more than the longest side), and the three interior angles must add to exactly $180^\circ$. Once a triangle exists, the way the parts are arranged decides uniqueness: SSS, SAS, ASA, and AAS each pin down a single triangle, AAA (three angles, no side) fixes the shape but not the size so it gives infinitely many triangles, and SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) is the ambiguous case that can give zero, one, or two triangles.

items.prompt: Can a triangle be drawn with side lengths $4\text{ cm}$, $5\text{ cm}$, and $11\text{ cm}$? Explain using the triangle inequality.

steps: The triangle inequality says the two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest side.
Identify the longest side: $11\text{ cm}$. The two shorter sides are $4\text{ cm}$ and $5\text{ cm}$.
Add the two shorter sides: $4 + 5 = 9$.
Compare to the longest side: $9 < 11$, so the two short sides cannot reach across the long side.
Because $4 + 5 < 11$, no triangle can be formed.
solution.answer: No triangle. Since $4 + 5 = 9 < 11$, the triangle inequality fails.

items.prompt: Can a triangle have interior angles measuring $40^\circ$, $60^\circ$, and $90^\circ$? Explain using the angle-sum property.

steps: The three interior angles of any triangle must add to exactly $180^\circ$.
Add the given angles: $40^\circ + 60^\circ + 90^\circ = 190^\circ$.
Compare to $180^\circ$: $190^\circ \ne 180^\circ$.
Because the angles do not sum to $180^\circ$, they cannot be the interior angles of a triangle.
solution.answer: No triangle. The angles sum to $190^\circ$, not $180^\circ$.

items.prompt: A set of conditions gives a triangle with angles $50^\circ$, $60^\circ$, and $70^\circ$, but no side length is specified. Does this determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle? Name the criterion.

steps: First check feasibility with the angle sum: $50^\circ + 60^\circ + 70^\circ = 180^\circ$, so a triangle is possible.
Notice that only three angles are given and no side length is fixed. This is the AAA condition.
Three angles fix the shape of the triangle but not its size, so you can scale the triangle up or down and still satisfy all three angle conditions.
Therefore infinitely many similar triangles meet these conditions.
solution.answer: More than one triangle (infinitely many similar triangles). This is the AAA condition, which fixes shape but not size.

items.prompt: A triangle is described by two sides of $6\text{ cm}$ and $8\text{ cm}$ with an included angle of $40^\circ$ between them. Is the triangle unique? Which congruence criterion applies?

steps: Identify the parts given: two sides ($6\text{ cm}$ and $8\text{ cm}$) and the angle between them ($40^\circ$).
An angle that sits between the two given sides is called the included angle.
Two sides with the included angle is the SAS (Side-Angle-Side) condition.
SAS fixes the lengths of both sides and the exact opening between them, so only one triangle can be built.
Therefore the triangle is unique.
solution.answer: Unique triangle. The condition is SAS (two sides with the included angle).

items.prompt: Using a ruler and protractor, you want to construct a triangle with a $7\text{ cm}$ base, a $45^\circ$ angle at one end of the base, and a $60^\circ$ angle at the other end. Describe the construction and state whether the triangle is unique.

steps: Draw the base: use the ruler to draw a segment exactly $7\text{ cm}$ long. Label its endpoints $A$ and $B$.
At endpoint $A$, place the protractor and draw a ray making a $45^\circ$ angle with the base.
At endpoint $B$, place the protractor and draw a ray making a $60^\circ$ angle with the base, opening toward the same side as the first ray.
Mark the point where the two rays cross as $C$; triangle $ABC$ is the result.

The condition is two angles with the side between them (ASA), which determines a unique triangle. You can check feasibility: the third angle is $180^\circ - 45^\circ - 60^\circ = 75^\circ$, a valid angle.
solution.answer: A unique triangle. The condition is ASA (two angles with the included side).

items.prompt: Can a triangle be drawn with side lengths $3\text{ cm}$, $4\text{ cm}$, and $7\text{ cm}$? Explain.
items.hint: Add the two shorter sides and compare to the longest side. Watch for the boundary case where the sum equals the longest side.

steps: The longest side is $7\text{ cm}$; the two shorter sides are $3\text{ cm}$ and $4\text{ cm}$.
Add the two shorter sides: $3 + 4 = 7$.
Compare: $7 = 7$, so the two short sides exactly meet the long side instead of rising above it.
When the sum equals the longest side, the figure collapses flat into a straight segment, so it is degenerate and not a true triangle.
solution.answer: No triangle. Since $3 + 4 = 7$ equals the longest side, the figure is a straight segment (degenerate).

items.prompt: Two of a triangle's interior angles measure $35^\circ$ and $85^\circ$. Find the third angle, and state whether such a triangle can exist.
items.hint: The three interior angles must total $180^\circ$. Subtract the two known angles from $180^\circ$.

steps: The angles must sum to $180^\circ$: third angle $= 180^\circ - 35^\circ - 85^\circ$.
Compute: $180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ$.
The third angle is $60^\circ$, which is a positive angle less than $180^\circ$, so the triangle is feasible.
solution.answer: The third angle is $60^\circ$, and the triangle can exist.

items.prompt: A triangle is described by two angles of $50^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ and a side of $9\text{ cm}$ that is not between those two angles. Does this determine a unique triangle? Name the criterion.
items.hint: Two angles and any one side fix the triangle. When the side is not the included side, the criterion is AAS.

steps: Two angles are given, so the third angle is forced: $180^\circ - 50^\circ - 60^\circ = 70^\circ$.
Once all three angles and one actual side length are known, the size is locked in.
Because the given side is not between the two given angles, the condition is AAS (Angle-Angle-Side).
AAS determines a unique triangle.
solution.answer: Unique triangle. The condition is AAS.

items.prompt: Conditions: angles $30^\circ$, $70^\circ$, and $80^\circ$ with no side length given. Does this determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle? Explain.
items.hint: First check the angle sum, then notice whether any actual length is fixed.

steps: Check the angle sum: $30^\circ + 70^\circ + 80^\circ = 180^\circ$, so a triangle is possible.
Only three angles are given and no side length is specified; this is the AAA condition.
AAA fixes the shape but not the size, so the triangle can be drawn at any scale.
Therefore there are infinitely many similar triangles, not a unique one.
solution.answer: More than one triangle (infinitely many similar triangles), because AAA fixes only the shape.

items.prompt: The two shorter sides of a triangle measure $6\text{ cm}$ and $10\text{ cm}$. Find the range of possible lengths for the third side $c$.
items.hint: The third side must satisfy $|a - b| < c < a + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are the two given sides.

steps: The third side must be shorter than the sum of the other two: $c < 6 + 10 = 16$.
The third side must also be longer than the difference of the other two: $c > |10 - 6| = 4$.
Combine both conditions: $4 < c < 16$.
Any length strictly between $4\text{ cm}$ and $16\text{ cm}$ produces a valid triangle.
